vignette:
He is a quiet man, the kind who blends into a room. At forty-six, he still has the lean frame of a runner, though he stopped jogging months ago. He works as a graphic designer for a midsized advertising firm, and his colleagues know him as reliable if a little withdrawn. His wife says he used to hum while he worked at his drafting table. That was before.

The trouble began on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. He was driving home from a client meeting, taking a shortcut through a neighborhood he didn’t usually use. He stopped at a traffic light, and a patrol car pulled up behind him, lights flashing but no siren. He didn’t think much of it—maybe they were just passing through. Then the officer’s voice came over the loudspeaker, telling him to turn off the engine and keep his hands visible. His heart kicked. He did as he was told. Two officers approached, one on each side, shouting for him to exit the vehicle. He fumbled with the seatbelt. He was pulled out, face pressed against the cold hood, hands wrenched behind his back. They said he matched the description of a robbery suspect—a man in his forties, dark jacket, driving a dark sedan. It took fifteen minutes for dispatch to confirm he wasn’t the one. The officers apologized, curt and flat. No charges. No paperwork. Just a sore wrist and a jacket that smelled of asphalt.

That was eighteen months ago. He still hears the shouting sometimes, not in the room but behind his eyes. It comes when he’s trying to focus on a layout, a sudden jolt of adrenaline that makes his fingers freeze over the keyboard. He avoids driving through that neighborhood now, even if it means a forty-minute detour. His wife suggested they take a weekend trip to the countryside last spring, but he couldn’t bring himself to sit in a car for more than thirty minutes without his hands starting to tremble.

He works from home most days. The office has an open plan, and he can’t tolerate having anyone behind him. He asked for a cubicle in the corner, facing the door, but even then he flinches when a coworker walks up too fast. He told his boss it was a neck issue. At his drafting table, he will sometimes stop mid-task, staring at a blank screen, trying to remember what he was doing. The images come whether he wants them or not: the metallic taste of fear, the hard pressure of the handcuffs, the officer’s voice saying “keep your hands where I can see them” even after they knew it was a mistake.

He has started double-checking his rearview mirror obsessively. At traffic lights, he leaves a car length of space, always watching for police cars. He no longer listens to police scanners or crime podcasts—he used to enjoy them. Now the sirens in his neighbor’s TV show make him freeze mid-bite of dinner. He tells his wife he’s fine, that it was just a misunderstanding, that he should get over it. But he can’t.

Sleep is thin. He wakes at 3:17 AM most nights, heart pounding, a vague sense of something about to happen. He checks the locks, then checks them again. He has started sketching with heavy black lines, angular, sharp. His latest project—a brochure for a local charity—feels hollow. The colors don’t sing the way they used to. He misses that. He doesn’t say it out loud. He just sits at the table, hands still, waiting for something he can’t name.
